DISCUSSION
The aim of this study was to describe changes in the Tsk of the knee
ROI throughout the return-to-play process after ACL reconstruction
in football players. To the knowledge of these authors, this is the first
study to use thermography to describe the evolution of knee tem-
perature according to the chronological stages of the injury in football
players. Moreover, it is the first study to establish Tsk throughout
their rehabilitation process as one more criterion to achieve a safe
RTP.

Return-to-play criteria based on infrared thermography during anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation in football players. Biol Sport. 2025;42(2):161-167.",
   "doi":"10.5114/biolsport.2025.144295",
   "abstract":"Descriptive longitudinal study of knee skin temperature asymmetry measured by infrared thermography in 30 football players (male 23, female 7) during rehabilitation and return-to-play after ACL reconstruction, from day 2 to day 365. A linear mixed model with athlete as a random effect was used, and asymmetry decreased over time after surgery, with no significant sex effect.",
   "tldr":"Knee skin temperature asymmetry after ACL reconstruction fell steadily over the first year, which may help staff track healing between rehabilitation stages. The study does not show that any temperature value marks a safe return to play.",
   "methods":"Thermal images of the anterior legs were taken at days 2, 9, 20, 35, 63, 126, 187, 274 and 365 after surgery, using a FLIR T530 camera and standard room conditions. Knee regions of interest were extracted with ThermoHuman software, and the injured minus healthy knee asymmetry was modelled with linear mixed models (Day and Sex as fixed effects, athlete as random effect), with the best model selected by AIC.",
   "findings":"Asymmetry decreased with time after surgery (-0.01 degrees C per day, P < 0.01, Table 2), with a model intercept of 1.92 degrees C. Sex was not significant (estimate 0.14, P = 0.18). The authors report a model-based estimate of 2.52 degrees C at surgery and 1.62 degrees C at day 90, and a final asymmetry of 0.46 +/- 0.13 degrees C, still above healthy-knee values. The study did not record actual return-to-play dates, so the temperature values were not linked to return outcomes.",
   "limitations":"The study has no return-to-play dates or reinjury outcomes, and no other rehabilitation or performance measures were collected. Clubs used different rehabilitation protocols and leagues were heterogeneous, and the sample includes only players who met functional criteria in the first year. The authors also acknowledge the camera's stated accuracy of about +/-2 degrees C and the sensitivity of absolute temperature to environment.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff can track the injured minus healthy knee temperature asymmetry at set time points after ACL reconstruction, and look for a steady decline as a sign of healing. The authors suggest using it alongside other markers, such as thigh temperature and strength balance, but a single asymmetry value should not be read as a clearance threshold.",
   "athleteDev":"Thermography could give performance staff an extra monitoring point in the months after ACL reconstruction, especially around day 35 to 187 when the study shows the asymmetry trend. It should sit alongside strength, hop and load data rather than replace them.",
   "rtp":"The study can support monitoring of knee inflammation and recovery between rehabilitation stages after ACL reconstruction. It cannot be used as a return-to-play clearance criterion, because it has no outcome data linking thermal asymmetry to safe return or reinjury, and the authors did not validate any threshold."
 }
}

75	    The present scoping review aims to describe the available criteria to                                 Received 26 April 2024

77	    erations and new research questions, and provide information to                                       KEYWORDS

80	    sional male football. The following electronic databases were                                         rehabilitation; sports

82	    using keywords related to HSI in elite football. All types of studies

276	Assessment of risk of bias
277	The study selection of the present scoping review included a variety of study typologies.
278	The review aims to describe all the studies published on the specific topic, including case
279	reports and opinion papers. Therefore, due to the descriptive nature of this paper and the
280	heterogeneity of the articles, no assessment tools were utilized to evaluate the internal
281	validity of the included studies as described in previous scoping reviews (Rambaud et al.,
282	2018).

287	Study identification and selection
288	The electronic database search yielded 1026 records (Figure 1). The data were
289	imported to the “Rayyan – the intelligent systematic review” web app (www.rayyan.
290	ai). Duplicates (n = 453) were removed automatically. The remaining 573 titles and
291	abstracts were screened for their relevance. Fifty-two studies were included for full-text
292	review. Following the full-text inspection, 33 articles were removed for one of the
293	following reasons: RTP criteria were not described (n = 11), the participants were not
294	professional male football players aged 17 to 45 (n = 11), RTP criteria were not football
295	specific (n = 9), no hamstring specific (n = 1). Nineteen studies were included in the
296	final scoping review.

309	Absence of pain

311	Dunlop et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2022; Taberner et al., 2020, 2022; van der Horst et al.,
312	2017; Zambaldi et al., 2017). Delvaux et al. (2013) used a bespoke questionnaire to
313	interview 37 sports medicine physicians from French and Belgian male professional foot­
314	ball clubs about the most important RTP criteria after an HSI. Complete absence of pain
315	was indicated as the most important criterion because the pain would indicate “incom­
316	plete injury healing”. Dunlop et al. (2020) used an online survey to interview practitioners
317	responsible for the RTP programme from 131 professional football clubs. The majority
318	(57%) identified the absence of pain during clinical evaluation (e.g., on palpation, during

a consensus was obtained. When required, all the authors shared opinions in case of
doubts during the selection process.



Data extraction process
The selected studies were stored in a Microsoft Excel datasheet indicating the following
variables: year and country of publication, type of journal (sports medicine or not), study
design, typology of sample (only professional football), age of the sample, type of ham­
string injury, criteria used to RTP. The Excel datasheet is available in the supplementary
material.



Assessment of risk of bias
The study selection of the present scoping review included a variety of study typologies.
The review aims to describe all the studies published on the specific topic, including case
reports and opinion papers. Therefore, due to the descriptive nature of this paper and the
heterogeneity of the articles, no assessment tools were utilized to evaluate the internal
validity of the included studies as described in previous scoping reviews (Rambaud et al.,
2018).
                                                           RESEARCH IN SPORTS MEDICINE      5


Results
Study identification and selection
The electronic database search yielded 1026 records (Figure 1). The data were
imported to the “Rayyan – the intelligent systematic review” web app (www.rayyan.
ai). Duplicates (n = 453) were removed automatically. The remaining 573 titles and
abstracts were screened for their relevance. Fifty-two studies were included for full-text
review. Following the full-text inspection, 33 articles were removed for one of the
following reasons: RTP criteria were not described (n = 11), the participants were not
professional male football players aged 17 to 45 (n = 11), RTP criteria were not football
specific (n = 9), no hamstring specific (n = 1). Nineteen studies were included in the
final scoping review.



RTP criteria
The studies and the RTP criteria included in this scoping review are summarized in Table 1.
Due to the differences between the criteria, we proposed to group the criteria into three
categories: clinical, strength and performance. Table 2 shows the criteria grouped into
these three categories.



Clinical criteria
Absence of pain
Absence of pain was utilized in seven studies as an RTP criterion (Delvaux et al., 2013;
Dunlop et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2022; Taberner et al., 2020, 2022; van der Horst et al.,
2017; Zambaldi et al., 2017). Delvaux et al. (2013) used a bespoke questionnaire to
interview 37 sports medicine physicians from French and Belgian male professional foot­
ball clubs about the most important RTP criteria after an HSI. Complete absence of pain
was indicated as the most important criterion because the pain would indicate “incom­
plete injury healing”. Dunlop et al. (2020) used an online survey to interview practitioners
responsible for the RTP programme from 131 professional football clubs. The majority
(57%) identified the absence of pain during clinical evaluation (e.g., on palpation, during
strength and flexibility tests) and/or following functional performance testing (e.g., run­
ning mechanic drills, low-moderate speed running) as the most important criterion for
return to high-speed running within the RTP continuum described in the study (return-to-
high-speed running, return-to-train, return-to-play, return-to-performance). The defini­
tions of the RTP continuum phases are summarized in Table 3. Similar results were
presented by van der Horst et al. (2017) in their Delphi study. Fifty-eight experts from
28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence worldwide identified the absence of pain on
palpation of the hamstrings, on strength and flexibility testing and on functional perfor­
mance as important criterion for RTRun. In the case study presented by Taberner et al.
(2022), the professional football player was deemed ready to return to on-field rehabilita­
tion following a semimembranosus proximal-free tendon injury once pain was absent. In

545	 Criteria                                                       Definition
546	 Return-to-high-speed  The period between hamstring injury occurring and the player being cleared to run on-field
547	    running              and progresses to high-speed running
548	 Return-to-train       When the player is allowed to return to on-field unrestricted training
549	 Return-to-play        When the player is cleared to return to competitive match-play with the team (whether
550	                         selected or not)
551	 Return-to-performance When the player returned to pre-injury levels of performance (or higher)
552	
553	
554	
555	surgical repair described by Taberner et al. (2020), absence of pain was used 18 weeks
556	post-surgery to clear the player to return to unrestricted team training.
557	
558	Hamstring flexibility
559	Hamstring flexibility was utilized in five studies as an RTP criterion (Delvaux et al., 2013;
560	Dunlop et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2022; van der Horst et al., 2017; Zambaldi et al., 2017). In
561	their survey, Delvaux et al. (2013) reported that Hamstring muscle flexibility represented
562	the fourth most relevant RTP criterion on a list of 12 criteria. Dunlop et al. (2020) reported
563	that hamstring flexibility was the third most appropriate test to clear a player for return to
564	running following an HSI. van der Horst et al. (2017) reported that a consensus about
565	using hamstring flexibility as an RTP criterion was reached. The experts agreed that a 0%–
566	                                                            RESEARCH IN SPORTS MEDICINE       11
567	
568	
569	10% difference between injured and uninjured leg or compared with preinjury data is
570	required. They also reached consensus that hamstring flexibility should be assessed by
571	means of both the active and the passive straight leg raise test. Zambaldi et al. (2017)
572	reported that all the Delphi study participants agreed that full hamstring flexibility is
573	necessary for a safe RTP, but the best method to assess it has not been specified.
574	
575	Medical staff clearance
576	Medical staff clearance was described in two studies (Dunlop et al., 2020; van der
577	Horst et al., 2017). Although Dunlop et al. (2020) reported that 80% of Premier
578	League teams surveyed used a shared decision-making approach, others have
579	shown that responsibility belongs to the medical staff. Ninety-six teams (73%)
580	reported that medical staff were responsible for the RTP clearance. In addition, the
581	teams revealed that ≥87% of the time across the different stages of RTP at least one
582	medical practitioner was consulted. Similarly, in the Delphi study conducted by van
583	der Horst et al. (2017) the experts’ panel reached an agreement on medical staff
584	clearance as a criterion for RTP.
585	
586	Psychological readiness
587	Psychological readiness was included in seven studies (Delvaux et al., 2013; Dunlop et al.,
588	2020; Garcia et al., 2022; Taberner et al., 2020, 2022; van der Horst et al., 2017; Zambaldi
589	et al., 2017). The physicians questioned in the Delvaux et al. (2013) study ranked the
590	subjective feeling reported by the player as the third criterion out of the list of 12 options.
591	Psychological criteria were considered for RTP by the experts in the survey by Dunlop
592	et al. (2020) and the Delphi studies by van der Horst et al. (2017) and Zambaldi et al.
593	(2017). All three studies highlighted the importance of psychological readiness for RTP,
594	suggesting that factors such as fear of pain, fear of reinjury and higher motivation could
595	impact the outcome. However, in professional football, there are no validated tools to
596	measure psychological readiness following a hamstring injury (van der Horst et al., 2017).
597	In the two case studies (Taberner et al., 2020, 2022), the authors reported that subjective
598	feedback from the player was part of the criteria used alongside a combination of clinical,
599	strength and performance criteria.
600	
601	Surgeon’s opinion
602	The surgeon’s opinion was only included in one study (Taberner et al., 2020). In this case,
603	study on rehabilitating a surgically managed semimembranosus injury, the authors
604	utilized the surgeon’s opinion as a criterion to clear the player to return to team training.
605	
606	Imaging as RTP criterion
607	Imaging was included as an RTP criterion in three studies (Baldock et al., 2021; Taberner
608	et al., 2020, 2022). Baldock et al. (2021) presented three cases of HSI with intramuscular
609	tendon involvement. They concluded that the healing of those injuries can be accurately
610	seen on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans and that this information should be
611	used as a criterion for RTP. Taberner et al. (2020) utilized healing and maturation on MRI
612	scans as one of the criteria to return the player to team training. Finally, Taberner et al.
613	(2022) used additional imaging (ultrasound) to clear the player’s transition into the foot­
614	ball-specific phases of the control-to-chaos continuum framework (Taberner et al., 2019).
615	 12      P. PERNA ET AL.
616	
617	
618	Strength criteria
619	Strength criteria were reported in nine studies (Delvaux et al., 2013; Dunlop et al., 2020;
620	Garcia et al., 2022; Moreno-Pérez et al., 2020; Taberner et al., 2020, 2022; Tol et al., 2014;
621	van der Horst et al., 2017; Zambaldi et al., 2017). Delvaux et al. (2013), Dunlop et al. (2020)
622	and Zambaldi et al. (2017) all agreed that strength objective measures should be used as
623	an RTP criterion. However, none of the studies reported which tests should be used.
624	Conversely, the experts in the Delphi study by van der Horst et al. (2017) did not reach
625	a consensus on the use of eccentric strength as a criterion to support the RTP decision, but
626	a consensus was reached that other contraction modalities should not be included as
627	a criterion to support the RTP decision. In the van der Horst et al. (2017) study, single leg
628	bridge was identified as a performance test to assess readiness to RTP.

630	(Nordic hamstring) and two isometric hamstring tests (15° knee flexion and 90:20). The

821	rehabilitation process goes through phases of progression until the return to playing

823	and indicate the ability to progress to the next phase. The review also included different

825	variability among the evidence. To be included in this review, studies had to be published in

832	sports that are potentially used in practice but not reported here. Finally, this scoping review
833	(because of its characteristics) does not provide guidelines for clinical practice (Munn et al.,
834	2018), in particular, it was beyond the scope of this review to assess the validity of RTP tests

 "evidenceSummary":"A scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus that included 19 studies of return-to-play criteria after hamstring strain in professional male football. The studies were surveys, Delphi studies, cohort and case studies, one randomized trial and one cross-sectional study, and the criteria were grouped as clinical (absence of pain in seven studies), strength (nine studies) and performance (six studies). The authors report heterogeneous criteria, with no validated return-to-play tools for psychological readiness, and a single trial in which 67% of players had at least one isokinetic deficit over 10% at return.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The authors did not appraise the risk of bias of the included studies, and the included evidence is mostly expert opinion, case reports and small retrospective cohorts.  "synthesisCaution":"Staff could take the grouped criteria as a validated return-to-play battery, when the authors state that no criterion has been validated and that the review does not assess the validity of any test.",
 "paper":{

   "doi":"10.1080/15438627.2024.2439274",
   "abstract":"Scoping review of the criteria used to determine return to play after a hamstring strain injury in professional male football. Four databases were searched, and 19 studies were included and grouped into clinical, strength and performance criteria, with clinical criteria further split into absence of pain, flexibility, medical clearance, psychological readiness, surgeon's opinion and imaging.",
   "tldr":"Return-to-play after hamstring injury in professional football is guided by a mix of clinical, strength and performance criteria, but no criterion set has been validated. Staff should combine criteria in their battery and involve several disciplines in the decision.",
   "methods":"Scoping review following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on OSF in June 2023. Two reviewers screened PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus records (1026 identified, 573 screened after duplicates removed, 19 included), and extracted design, sample, injury type and criteria. No risk-of-bias tool was applied.",
   "findings":"Of the 19 studies, absence of pain was used as a criterion in seven, hamstring flexibility in five, psychological readiness in seven, strength in nine and performance in six. Imaging was a criterion in three studies, and the surgeon's opinion in one. One randomized trial (Tol et al.) found that 67% of players had at least one isokinetic deficit over 10% at return. MRI grade and the BAMIC classification were reported as predictors of time to return, with a 3-day rise in return time per BAMIC grade in one cohort.",
   "limitations":"The review did not appraise study quality, and the authors note the evidence is weighted toward surveys, Delphi studies and case reports. Only English-language studies were included, and the review does not assess test validity or the optimal test for each injury type and stage. The text and flow diagram disagree on the number of full texts screened (52 vs 51).",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff should use a combination of clinical, strength and performance criteria, and make the return decision with several disciplines involved. Strength testing should include hamstring isokinetic or isometric tests, and the authors note that the choice of test is not settled. Psychological readiness should be assessed, although no validated tool exists in this population.",
   "athleteDev":"For professional footballers returning from hamstring injury, the review supports a criteria-based battery that includes absence of pain, hamstring strength and flexibility, sport-specific performance and load monitoring. Performance staff should plan for the high re-injury risk noted in the introduction, rather than relying on a single test.",
   "rtp":"The review can inform the clinical, strength and performance criteria used in return-to-play planning after hamstring injury in professional football. It cannot be used to set a validated pass or fail threshold, and the authors state it does not provide clinical practice guidelines."
 }
}

 "identityCheck":"Title in text ('Review of WADA Prohibited Substances: Limited Evidence for Performance-Enhancing Effects') matches the filename (the filename's spelling of 'Effects' is a typo); this text is the same article as Q95 apart from running headers.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A review of PubMed-identified studies and reviews of the 23 substance classes on the 2018 WADA Prohibited List, using double-blind randomized trials in trained subjects as the main evidence standard. The authors report that 5 classes (anabolic agents, beta2-agonists, stimulants, glucocorticoids and beta-blockers) show evidence of enhancing actual sports performance, mainly strength or sprint performance, and growth hormone has similar evidence only in untrained subjects. The level 1 evidence base is 11 studies with 266 subjects, and the authors state there is no robust evidence of benefit for endurance performance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The search used PubMed alone with keyword combinations and reference checking, without PRISMA reporting, so study selection is not reproducible. Several cited studies had small samples, lacked a baseline or placebo comparison, or used untrained subjects, which the authors flag as limits on the conclusions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the finding that most classes lack evidence as proof that the substances do not improve performance, when the review states that many classes have no well-designed studies at all, which is not the same as evidence of no effect.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Heuberger JAAC, Cohen AF. Review of WADA Prohibited Substances: Limited Evidence for Performance-Enhancing Effects. Sports Med. 2019;49:525-539.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-018-1014-1",
   "abstract":"Review of the evidence for performance enhancement across the 23 substance classes on the 2018 WADA Prohibited List, using PubMed searches. Only 5 of 23 classes showed evidence of enhancing actual sports performance, with growth hormone showing similar evidence only in untrained subjects, and the evidence base is 11 studies with 266 subjects.",
   "tldr":"Most of the substances on the WADA Prohibited List have no convincing evidence of improving athletic performance in trained athletes. The few classes with evidence improve strength or sprint performance, and none improve endurance performance in the studies reviewed.",
   "methods":"Narrative review with a PubMed search using keyword combinations for each substance class, supplemented by reference lists. Evidence was graded by study design (double-blind randomized trials as level 1) and by training status (untrained, trained or highly trained), with actual performance tests preferred over surrogate markers.",
   "findings":"Five classes showed evidence of enhancing actual performance in trained subjects: anabolic agents (strength, from three studies with 91 volunteers), beta2-agonists (peak sprint power and muscle strength, from three studies with 39 volunteers), stimulants (strength, sprint and some running time-trial measures, from two studies in the text that the authors describe as mixed), glucocorticoids (specific strength tests and shuttle run time, from one study with 10 subjects on a surrogate marker) and beta-blockers (shooting accuracy, from one study of 33 subjects). Growth hormone improved sprint performance in untrained subjects only. The authors state there is no robust evidence that any class improves endurance performance, and 11 of 23 classes had no well-designed studies in trained subjects.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that the search was limited to PubMed, that the standard applied (level 1 evidence in trained subjects) excludes much of the older and less well-controlled literature, and that many studies were in untrained or small samples. They also state that effects on VO2max or time to exhaustion were treated as weak surrogate outcomes, and that the review cannot show what would happen in elite athletes or in sports not covered.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff who advise athletes on prohibited substances should treat the evidence as limited, and should not assume that a listed substance improves performance in a given sport. The authors note that clear evidence of no effect for a class would be useful to share with athletes, and that research to fill the gaps in the evidence base could be done in many areas.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance staff should not use this review to judge whether a listed substance helps a specific athlete, since most evidence concerns strength or sprint tasks in small trials. Any discussion of performance-enhancing claims should refer to the specific substance class and the study population.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable. The review does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and it cannot inform clearance decisions after injury."
